SMTO-PSM-0019 — A parameter with that name already exists

GUID: 3809b083-1943-4b4b-b5b1-7d640cc73e5c
Slug: parameter-duplicate
Domain: PSM · Subsystem: psm

What happened

  • SMTO couldn't save because the name you chose matches a parameter that already exists. Names that differ only in capital letters, spaces or dashes count as the same. Nothing was saved.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. In Parameter Store, type the name into Search parameters…. Remember that "My Server", "my-server" and "my_server" are the same name to SMTO. SMTO ignores capitals and treats spaces and dashes as underscores, so a similar-looking name may already exist.
  2. If you find it and it's the one you meant, open it and change it there instead of creating a new one. Editing the existing parameter keeps one copy, so your @ references keep working.
  3. If it's a different thing, change Key to a new name and select Save again. A different name lets both parameters exist side by side.

What success looks like

  • Parameter Store shows Saved and the list shows the parameter under the name you chose.

If it still fails

  • If no parameter with that name shows up but saving still fails, select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages SMTO. Don't delete other parameters to make room for the name.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • Parameter create or update raised a storage error containing 'UNIQUE' or 'constraint', which the route reports as a key conflict (usually another entry already has the same normalized key).

What this means

  • Parameter create/update catches an exception containing UNIQUE or constraint and translates it to a key-conflict response. Accepted parameter bindings preserve exact identity and revision. Validation does not authorize secret substitution, alias guessing or replay of earlier work; failed write confirmation requires reading the original stored state.

Why this can happen

  • Parameter create/update catches an exception containing UNIQUE or constraint and translates it to a key-conflict response.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect whether the proposed normalized key already exists; this broad exception mapping can also hide a different constraint failure.

How to fix it

  • Search Parameter Store for the normalized key (lowercase, spaces/dashes as underscores). If an entry already has it, edit that entry or pick a different key. If no entry matches, the constraint was something else: check the Server log for the underlying sqlite constraint error before retrying.
  • Inspect the existing key and underlying safe constraint diagnostic; choose a unique key only when a collision is confirmed.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the recorded cause, then inspect current state and existing receipts before requesting another attempt.

How to verify the fix

  • The actual constraint is established and a deliberate valid create/update succeeds.

What not to do

  • Do not repeatedly submit the same invalid input; correct the named constraint first.

Technical notes

  • Accepted parameter bindings preserve exact identity and revision. Validation does not authorize secret substitution, alias guessing or replay of earlier work; failed write confirmation requires reading the original stored state.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
